012 — .NET out-of-band security updates, October 2026: patch now

The one idea: On 25 October, Microsoft shipped an out-of-band (off-schedule) .NET security release. It fixes a Brotli decompression buffer overflow that may let an unauthenticated attacker read or corrupt process memory, plus a Linux tarball file-ownership flaw. It also completes two fixes from the 13 October release. Update to 8.0.33, 9.0.22, 10.0.14 or 11.0 RC3, and rebuild self-contained apps and containers.

Added 2026-10-27 · Released 2026-10-25 by Microsoft

1. What it is

CVE Area Platforms Impact
CVE-2026-111497 Brotli decompression buffer overflow All Information disclosure, denial of service or elevation of privilege; may let an unauthenticated attacker read or corrupt process memory
CVE-2026-114148 Unsafe file ownership in .NET tarballs Linux A local attacker could modify files and gain elevated privileges. On .NET 10/11 this affects source-build tarballs only; on .NET 8/9 it also affects ASP.NET Core tarballs
CVE-2026-70197 (re-released) SocketAsyncEventArgs memory corruption .NET 8–11 The 13 October fix was incomplete
CVE-2026-102870 (re-released) Blazor WebAssembly debugger .NET 10–11 The 13 October fix was incomplete

Fixed versions: .NET 8 → 8.0.33, .NET 9 → 9.0.22, .NET 10 → 10.0.14, .NET 11 → RC3. RC2 users should move to RC3. .NET Framework isn't affected.

2. Why it matters

  • Out-of-band means urgent. Microsoft normally ships .NET fixes on Patch Tuesday. An extra release twelve days later signals that it didn't want these issues to wait a month.
  • Brotli is on the request path. Your app is exposed if it uses ASP.NET Core request decompression, HttpClient automatic response decompression, or the System.IO.Compression Brotli APIs. Those decompression features are off by default, but many APIs turn them on to save bandwidth.
  • Patched hosts don't fix self-contained apps. A self-contained app or a container image carries its own runtime. It stays vulnerable until you rebuild it.

3. How it works

---
title: Who needs to do what after a .NET runtime fix
---
flowchart TD
    A{"How is the app deployed?"} -->|"Framework-dependent"| B["Install the patched runtime<br/>on the host, restart the app"]
    A -->|"Self-contained"| C["Rebuild and republish<br/>with the patched SDK"]
    A -->|"Container"| D["Rebuild from the updated<br/>.NET base image, redeploy"]
    A -->|"Linux tarball / source-build"| E["Fetch the refreshed tarball<br/>or source-build artefacts"]
    B --> V["Verify: dotnet --list-runtimes"]
    C --> V
    D --> V
    E --> V

The Brotli flaw is in decompression. A crafted compressed payload in a request or response can make the decoder write outside its buffer. That's why apps that decompress data from untrusted senders are the ones exposed.

4. How to use it

  1. Find your exposure. Search the code for UseRequestDecompression, AutomaticDecompression (on HttpClientHandler or SocketsHttpHandler), and BrotliStream or BrotliDecoder.
  2. Update the SDK and runtime to the fixed versions above. Pin the SDK in global.json if you use one.
  3. Rebuild and redeploy every self-contained app and container image. Point base images at the updated tag, for example mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:8.0, and rebuild without cache.
  4. Linux tarballs: on .NET 8/9, replace the ASP.NET Core runtime tarball. Source-build users fetch the new artefacts.
  5. Verify with dotnet --list-runtimes on hosts, and by checking the runtime version inside each image.
  6. On .NET 11 previews: move from RC2 to RC3 (see .NET 11 RC2).

In practice: put an "update .NET runtime" step in your base-image pipeline and let Dependabot or Renovate bump image tags. Then an out-of-band release is a rebuild, not a scramble.

5. Trade-offs and limits

  • No CVSS scores or exploit status are given in the post. Treat it as high priority anyway, because Microsoft says to update as soon as possible.
  • Turning decompression off is a stopgap, not a fix. It cuts the exposure on request and response paths, but direct BrotliStream use stays vulnerable until you patch.
  • Re-released CVEs mean the 13 October patch alone isn't enough. Check that hosts patched on 13 October have the newer build.
  • Adopt now or wait? Now. This is a security release, not a feature.

6. Where it fits

  • Security engineering: patch management and vulnerability response.
  • .NET deep dive: framework-dependent vs self-contained deployment.
  • App Service and hosting: how Azure hosting picks up runtime patches.
  • .NET 11 RC2: the preview line now superseded by RC3.

7. Questions to test yourself

  1. Why does patching the host not fix a self-contained .NET app?
  2. Which three features make an ASP.NET Core app process Brotli data from outside?
  3. What does "out-of-band" tell you about a security release?
  4. How do you prove a container image runs the patched runtime?
  5. Why would a CVE be "re-released", and what should you check as a result?

Sources
